summary: The narrator confronts Marcelina, who evades his question and speaks of Baalum as a special place of miracles, which he sees as a sign the community is brainwashed. He insists on taking Sarah home because her father is hospitalized and worried. Marcelina leads him to a stone bath building, once a royal bath fed by heated rocks and sacred cenote water, where incense fills a vaulted, latticed room with painted glyphs and a large stone platform.
one_line: In Baalum, the narrator urges Marcelina to take Sarah home to her hospitalized father, then is led to an ancient royal bath.
key_facts: Marcelina says Baalum has become a special place of miracles, and that a woman from outside can be part of it.
Marcelina says that when Sara was here before, she started teaching her to speak the community's language.
Marcelina says of the leader's medical powers: "Sometimes we don't understand how they happen, but he has great medical powers."
The narrator thinks the whole place has been brainwashed and that Marcelina has gone on mental autopilot.
The narrator says Sarah's father has been in the hospital and is not well, and that he spoke with him yesterday and found him very worried about her.
The narrator knows Dr. Goddard is treating Sarah but believes it is better to take her home immediately.
The narrator suspects the detour for the two women was a diversion or stall set up by Marcelina, who may have wanted to tell him something.
Marcelina calls families very important and says "We'll go now."
At the end of the long street, Marcelina stops in front of a stone building unlike the others and says it is where Sarah likes to be.
Marcelina says the building is the most sacred place in Baalum apart from the pyramid.
The building's doorway is a stone arch about five feet high, pointed at the top like a tiny Gothic cathedral.
Marcelina explains the building was once the royal bath, where heated rocks were brought in with spring water from a sacred cenote.
The roof is stone latticework that lets gray daylight filter through.
Incense rises from pots along the floor, and the room has carved and colored glyphs on its walls.
At the far end is a large stone platform embossed with carved and painted classical scenes and glyphs.
